source_text: At id esse testantur frequentata vitia et severa iudicia; constitit ergo esse peccatum. Quaerimus quid sit; utrum corpus aliquod sit, quod ex multis compositum videatur; an singulare quiddam, sicut unum aliquod elementum, vel per cogitationem a reliquorum communione purgatum. Porro nihil horum est. Quid est ergo? Appetitus liberae voluntatis, quem prohibet iustitia; vel, ut definitione utamur priore: Voluntas faciendi quod iustitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere. Considera ergo, utrum extra terminos definitionis huius peccatum nequeat inveniri, ne alibi vagetur, quod nos comprehensum putamus. Consulamus ergo iustitiam iudicantis, ut et illius testimonio clareat, utrum bene cinctum sit his limitibus genus omne peccati. Imputatne Deus quod scit non posse vitari? At nulla iustitia est, et summa deformitas; immo si hoc fiat, non puniuntur peccata, sed crescunt. A iusto enim iudice culpa puniri solet; ea si in ipsum arbitrum iustitiae corruptione pervadat, vindicata est de iudice, non punita. Non ergo imputat iustitia in peccatum, nisi unde liberum est abstinere. Liberum autem dici non potest, nisi quod sine aliquo inevitabili naturalium coactu, in iure emancipatae constiterit voluntatis. Optime ergo est finitum et plene: Peccatum est voluntas faciendi quod iustitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere. His ergo partibus absolutis, quaeratur unde sit, quod perturbatissime ante has definitiones fuerat inquisitum. Unde est ergo peccatum? Respondeo: De libera voluntate facientis.
pass_a_gloss: But frequented vices and severe judgments testify that it is; it stood therefore that there is sin. We ask what it is; whether it is some body, which may seem composed from many; or something singular, as some one element, or purged by thought from the communion of the rest. Further it is none of these. What is it therefore? An appetite of free will, which justice forbids; or, that we may use the earlier definition: A will of doing what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain. Consider therefore whether sin cannot be found outside the bounds of this definition, lest that wander elsewhere which we think comprehended. Let us therefore consult the justice of the one judging, so that by his testimony also it may be clear whether the whole genus of sin is well girt with these limits. Does God impute what he knows cannot be avoided? But there is no justice, and the highest deformity; nay if this is done, sins are not punished, but they grow. For by a just judge fault is accustomed to be punished; if that pervades the arbiter of justice himself by corruption, it has been avenged from the judge, not punished. Justice therefore does not impute into sin except that from which it is free to abstain. But it cannot be called free except what, without some inevitable coercion of natural things, has stood in the right of an emancipated will. Most well therefore is it finished and fully: Sin is a will of doing what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain. These parts therefore having been finished, let it be asked from where is that which had been inquired most confusedly before these definitions. From where therefore is sin? I reply: From the free will of the one doing.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: Repeated vices and severe judgments testify that it does. It is therefore established that sin exists. We ask what it is: whether it is some body visibly composed of many elements, or some single thing, like one element considered in thought apart from its combination with the others. But it is none of these. What is it, then? An appetite of free will which justice prohibits. Or, to use the earlier definition: the will to do what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain. Consider, then, whether sin can be found outside the boundaries of this definition, lest what we suppose contained be wandering elsewhere. Let us consult the judge’s justice, so that its testimony too may establish whether every kind of sin has been properly enclosed by these limits.

Does God impute what he knows cannot be avoided? That would be no justice, but the greatest disgrace. Indeed, if this occurred, sins would not be punished but increased. A just judge ordinarily punishes guilt. If guilt invaded the judge himself through the corruption of justice, it would have taken vengeance upon the judge, not been punished. Justice therefore imputes nothing as sin except what one is free to avoid. But nothing can be called free unless, without any unavoidable compulsion of natural forces, it lies within the authority of a will possessing its own freedom. The definition is therefore excellent and complete: sin is the will to do what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain. With these points resolved, let us ask where it comes from—a question asked in great disorder before these definitions. Where, then, does sin come from? I answer: from the doer’s free will.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
